title: Effective and responsible advice, recommendation and sale of agrochemical products

lessons.title: The regulatory and ethical framework
lessons.html:
The adviser's responsibility

Agrochemical advisers, sales agronomists and co-op technical staff strongly influence what farmers apply to crops, animals and the environment. A wrong recommendation can cause crop damage, residue rejections, worker poisoning, environmental harm, resistance and legal liability. Responsible advice combines technical competence, legal compliance and ethics.

Legal framework

  • Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act 36 of 1947: agricultural remedies must be registered and used only as the label directs. The label is a legal document: crop, pest, dosage, method, pre-harvest interval, re-entry and safety instructions are binding.
  • Off-label recommendations (use on an unregistered crop or pest, or at a different rate) are not permitted under the Act. Advise only within registered uses.
  • Pest control operators applying remedies for reward must be registered as required under Act 36 of 1947.
  • OHS Act 85 of 1993 and the regulations on hazardous chemical agents govern worker exposure.
  • National Water Act 36 of 1998 and NEMA 107 of 1998 address pollution and environmental duty of care.
  • Export markets impose maximum residue limits (MRLs) that may differ from local limits; advisers must know the destination market's requirements.

Professional standards

Industry bodies such as CropLife South Africa promote training and codes of conduct for responsible use, and many advisers are registered through the relevant professional or industry schemes. Keep your training current.

Ethics

  • Recommend what the problem needs, not what earns the highest commission.
  • Disclose commercial interests.
  • Say so when chemical control is not justified or when another product, method or adviser would serve the client better.
  • Never downplay hazards to make a sale.

lessons.title: Diagnosing problems and making recommendations
lessons.html:
A sound recommendation starts in the field

Diagnosis

  1. Visit the field or examine good samples and photographs.
  2. Identify the pest, disease, weed or deficiency correctly, using a laboratory or specialist where uncertain. Many symptoms look alike: herbicide drift, nutrient deficiency and virus can be confused.
  3. Assess severity and distribution: is it above the economic threshold?
  4. Consider crop stage, weather, previous applications, resistance history and the market the crop is going to.

Integrated pest management first

Consider cultural, biological and mechanical options before or alongside chemicals: resistant cultivars, rotation, sanitation, beneficial insects, pheromone traps, mating disruption. Chemicals are most effective when used as part of an IPM programme.

Choosing a product

  • Registered for that crop and that target.
  • Appropriate mode of action, rotating groups to manage resistance according to resistance management guidelines (e.g. IRAC, FRAC, HRAC groupings).
  • Least hazardous effective option for workers, bees, natural enemies and water.
  • Pre-harvest interval compatible with harvest dates and export MRLs.
  • Compatible with tank-mix partners, as stated on labels.
  • Cost-effective: product cost versus expected yield or quality benefit.

The written recommendation

Provide a written recommendation stating: client and field, crop and growth stage, target, product and registration number, dosage and water volume per label, application method and equipment, timing and weather conditions, pre-harvest interval and re-entry period, PPE, environmental precautions such as buffer zones and bee protection, and follow-up monitoring. Keep a copy: it protects both client and adviser.

Calculations

Double-check product quantity per tank and per hectare. A decimal error can destroy a crop or exceed residue limits. Ask the farmer to confirm sprayer calibration.

lessons.title: Responsible selling, stewardship and follow-up
lessons.html:
Beyond the sale

At the point of sale

  • Sell only registered products in original, intact, labelled packaging.
  • Confirm the buyer understands the label, especially for highly toxic products; explain PPE, mixing and first aid information on the label.
  • Do not decant products into unlabelled containers.
  • Store products in the shop according to legal and safety requirements: separate from food and feed, ventilated, bunded, with spill kits and fire equipment.
  • Keep sales records including product, batch and client.

Product stewardship

Stewardship covers the whole life cycle: transport, storage, use, empty container management and disposal of obsolete stock. Promote triple rinsing and return of containers through recognised collection schemes. Help clients dispose of obsolete stock through licensed hazardous waste services.

Worker and community safety

Advise on PPE, training of operators, medical surveillance where required for certain chemical classes, and emergency procedures. If poisoning is suspected, the person must be removed from exposure, contaminated clothing removed, skin washed with plenty of water, and medical help obtained with the product label. Advisers should know the poison information centre numbers. Hands-on first aid training by an accredited provider is required for responders.

Follow-up and evaluation

Revisit the field to evaluate efficacy and crop safety. Record outcomes and possible resistance or failures and report suspected product failures to the registration holder. Use results to improve future recommendations.

Handling complaints

Investigate complaints promptly, review the recommendation and application records, and take samples where needed. Be honest about errors.

Key points

  • The label is a legal document; recommend only registered uses.
  • Diagnose correctly and apply IPM principles first.
  • Choose products for efficacy, safety, resistance management and market MRLs.
  • Give written, checked recommendations and keep records.
  • Practise stewardship from sale to container disposal and follow up results.

quiz.question: What is the legal status of an agrochemical label?

options.text: A legal document whose instructions are binding

quiz.question: Which is the correct response when a client asks for an off-label use?

options.text: Agree if the farmer signs a waiver
Recommend it verbally but not in writing

options.text: They are always the same as local limits
